scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the value carries its unit at the boundary (pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent) - the class that made a knob of 10 mean 1000%

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.detail: MEASURED AND FAILING - the edge layer's error envelope is not machine-readable, and it is not shaped like the db layer's. Two concrete defects, both measured against the local edge runtime this session: (1) an edge function's error body is {"error": "<prose>"} with NO machine-readable `code` field, so a caller can only pattern-match English to decide what happened - while the SAME platform's db layer returns {code, details, hint, message} for every failure class (400 bad column, 404 unknown table, 401 no grant), which a client CAN branch on. One product, two incompatible error contracts. (2) a routing 404 (unknown function name) is returned as **text/plain**, so `res.json()` THROWS rather than yielding an error object - the caller's catch block sees a SyntaxError about unexpected token, not a 404, and any code that checks `data.error` never runs. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: this is the layer behind the AI gateway, the orchestrators, OCR/voice capture and report generation. A client that treats db and edge errors alike - which the identical-looking `.error` property invites - will mishandle one of them, and the failure mode is the one this bank keeps finding: an exception swallowed into an empty render, indistinguishable from a server that honestly answered nothing. LEFT OWED RATHER THAN GREEN, DELIBERATELY: the oracle asks that status and body AGREE and that the envelope be uniform, and it does not. Banking it green would be a false green; recording it owed with the diagnosis is the honest state. TO FINISH: return JSON for routing 404s (Content-Type application/json), and add a stable `code` alongside `error` in every edge error body, then re-walk. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Platform: 73 declared | 2 UNDECLARED | 5 latent | 0 MIXED-SCALE. Zero mixed-scale is the load-bearing number: no column stores fractions and whole percents in the same place. FOR THIS LAYER THE QUESTION IS GENUINELY OPEN, AND IT IS THE ONE LAYER THE SCHEMA CANNOT ANSWER. Every other boundary here carries values whose meaning is pinned by the column they come from. An AI-EMITTED number is not from a column - it is generated, and nothing in the schema constrains whether it arrives as hours or days, pesos or credits, a fraction or a whole percent. That is precisely the confusion this oracle exists to catch, and it is the one place the structural argument used for the other layers does NOT transfer. Recorded as owed rather than passed by association. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: capture an AI-produced quantity from this page's own AI path and check the emitted value against the unit its consumer assumes - the same before/after discipline the other provers use, applied to a generated number rather than a stored one.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_null_semantics.py - 286 client coalesce sites read out of the pages and joined against the SCHEMA, so each one is judged against whether its column can actually be NULL. ★THE ORACLE'S OWN EXAMPLE IS NUMERIC: 'NULL meant no cap in the DB and arrived as a cap of ZERO in the client'. So the sites are separated by what the substitution DESTROYS, not by how many there are: numeric-substitute (50) and boolean-substitute (3) turn an UNKNOWN into a definite value and are the real class; not-null-in-db (15) cannot fire because the column is NOT NULL; visible-placeholder (47) renders an em-dash or equivalent and is the CORRECT behaviour, not a defect; text-blank (171) collapses NULL to '' where both already render as nothing - a weaker concern, recorded but not charged as this oracle's failure. ★THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A REAL NULL, which is what stops a clean page from being a vacuous pass: the control column v_achievement_xp_log.source_id holds 77 live NULLs and is found. A detector that cannot see that cannot see any. ★AND THE LIVE COUNT IS SEPARATE FROM THE LATENT ONE: zero of these sites is misbehaving TODAY, because the columns concerned currently hold no NULLs (0/4, 0/95, 0/97 on the ones sampled). findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes resume_documents + resume_versions and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

evidence.asserts: What one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS: a value is not silently rewritten on the way in by something nobody named. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - values_survive_write extracts every trigger that assigns to NEW, classifies the rewrite by its STRUCTURE, and fails on any that belongs to no named class. It also measures the one class that can lose a person's work: every left(NEW.col, N) cap is read against the stored data, because a possible truncation and an actual one are different facts.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). It earned that by first FAILING on a trigger I had added earlier in this same session: tg_community_posts_moderation_fields, which restores flagged/pinned for a caller who is not a supervisor of that hive (migrations ...000063/64, after a reported author was found clearing their own flag). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. The fix was to teach the CLASSIFIER a new structural class, field-authorization-guard, not to rename my trigger guard_* to slip past a prefix check: the function's own docstring says widening the name allowlist until the gate goes green is bending the gate, and structure is what a rewrite DOES. The new class is detected on shape - every assignment restoring the column to its own prior value - so no outside value replaces the caller's and their other edits still land.

 | depends_on: tools/prove_values_survive_the_write.py

evidence.asserts: The field keeps its name and meaning across the seam: a rename on one side does not silently leave the other side reading a column that no longer exists. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - field_names_survive resolves every column name each page selects against the live relation and reports any that is gone. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS, 1,648 field names checked across all pages, none stale - and it earned that verdict by first FAILING. It caught asset-hub selecting `unit` from v_sensor_recent, a column the view does not have. That was not cosmetic: PostgREST REJECTS an unknown column rather than omitting it, so the sensor telemetry read was returning 400 and the panel got nothing at all, on every load. The data was never missing (sensor_readings carries unit, v_sensor_truth exposes it); only this view dropped it while being the one surface that asked for it, and meta was empty so no fallback carried it either. Fixed by migration ...000068 restoring the column to the view - appended last, because CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW can only add at the end. The gate also carries a control: an injected non-existent column must be reported, or a silent regex failure would read as a clean pass.

gate:field_names_survive (registered) | PASS: 1,648 names checked, 0 stale | caught this session: asset-hub select('unit') on v_sensor_recent -> PostgREST 400, whole sensor panel dead; fixed by migration 20260820000068 | control: injected non-existent column must be reported
 | depends_on: tools/prove_field_names_survive.py

HOW IT WAS MEASURED, browser-free. Every `x.col ?? 0` / `x.col || ''` site in this page's own source is cross-referenced against the LIVE CATALOG: the site counts only if `col` is really a column of a relation THIS PAGE READS, and only if it is NULLABLE there - a NOT NULL column makes the default unreachable defensive code, not a seam defect. Then the substitute is judged by WHAT IT DOES TO A READER rather than by its type. THE NARROWING IS THE WHOLE POINT, and the first run proves why: the 22 pages contain 1,557 sites matching this shape, and almost none are this defect - `opts.icon || ''` is a render option, `error.message || ''` is an exception, `target.value || ''` is the DOM, `postsRes.count ?? 0` is a PostgREST envelope field. Requiring a real nullable column of a relation the page reads cut 1,557 to 286. A tool that reported 1,557 would bury the handful that matter. (1) TEXT DEFAULTED TO '' IS NOT THIS DEFECT: `l.root_cause || ''` renders a BLANK, which is the honest presentation of 'not recorded' - '' is legal for text in the type system and meaningless in the domain, so nobody stores an empty root cause and no reader is deceived by one. That reclassified 171 sites. Both were read by hand rather than banked. That needs the enclosing expression, and inferring it by counting backticks across inline script is the brittle-validator trap this codebase has already been bitten by - a backtick inside a comment once took a whole page down. So the candidates are counted, named, and left for a human read, which is few enough to be honest work. PLATFORM RESULT for the client side, measured once: 286 qualifying sites across 22 pages - 171 text-to-blank (a reader sees absence, which is correct), 47 visible placeholders (a dash or a non-legal-for-the-type value, so visibly not a measurement), 15 on NOT NULL columns (unreachable), and 53 numeric/boolean substitutes. findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes resume_documents + resume_versions and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 4 reads answered 500, this page **asserts **'Nothing here yet.'** in place of the saved-resume list** while saying nothing about the failure. ON THIS PAGE THAT SENTENCE IS ABOUT A PERSON'S CAREER RECORD. The surface promises 'your files are read just to fill in your resume, then discarded'; a reader who has built resume versions and is told there is nothing here has reason to think the promise was not kept. A ZERO IS AN ANSWER. The reader cannot distinguish a backend fault from a true zero, and the page offers no sentence that would let them. NINE PAGES IN THE SAME SWEEP DO THIS PROPERLY, so the pattern is in-repo and this is unadopted rather than undesigned: hive - 'Could not reach your hive. Check your connection and refresh the page, or rejoin using your invite code.'; inventory - 'Stock levels are unknown right now, not zero.'; pm-scheduler - 'Overdue PMs are unknown right now, not zero. Reload before treating this plant as compliant.' Each names the domain consequence, not the status code. MEASURED BY ANSWERING EVERY READ WITH A 500 AT window.fetch AND READING WHAT THE PAGE SAYS NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request resolves to a synthetic `{"code":"500"}` with Content-Type application/json; `/auth/v1/` is untouched so the session survives, which is what makes this a SERVER fault rather than a dead network. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. Every claim below quotes the page's own visible sentence, collected from leaf-ish elements under a composed-visibility test (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) so hidden template copy cannot be mistaken for something a reader sees. TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS SWEEP WERE THROWN AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE NUMBERS HERE ARE TRUSTED. The first used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered live data - a registered service worker sits between page and transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. The second omitted the identity guard and returned byte-identical output for seven different pages (14,677 chars of marketing copy) because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. This version guards INSIDE the evaluate: expected uid, `location.pathname` ends in the page's own file, and body chars outside the 13,000-16,000 landing band - refusing rather than reporting. PLATFORM RESULT, all 22 pages: **9 state the failure in domain language** (hive, inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, index, skillmatrix, achievements, voice-journal, assistant) and **11 say nothing or assert a falsehood**. Only 2 offer a retry CONTROL (achievements, community); public-feed's was measured firing a real re-request and rendering 15 posts.

findings.detail: FINDING RETRACTED - NOT MEASURED. I recorded that resume 'renders Nothing here yet. in place of the saved-resume list' under a 500, and called it a false empty about a person's career record. **The identical sentence appears in the HEALTHY run.** With 9 reads succeeding and no injection at all, the page shows 'Nothing here yet.' - because this test account genuinely has no saved resume versions. So the sentence is the TRUE empty state, and what I attributed to a failed read is simply what the page says when there is nothing to list. The stakes I described (a promise about someone's documents) were real as a concern and unfounded as a measurement. WHAT A VALID MEASUREMENT NEEDS, so this is a recipe rather than a shrug: seed at least one `resume_versions` row for this worker so the healthy state is DISTINGUISHABLE from the empty one, then re-run failed-vs-healthy. Only a difference between those two runs is evidence about failure handling. Without a populated baseline this oracle cannot discriminate on this page at all - the same empty-denominator problem as an unarrived surface. WHY BOTH READINGS ARE UNSOUND, AND HOW IT WAS CAUGHT: the failed run and the HEALTHY control produced BYTE-COMPARABLE output. If injecting a 500 into every read changes nothing a reader can see, the injection did not reach what the page renders - so no verdict about its failure behaviour is available from that run, in either direction. Running the healthy control alongside is what exposed it; the original sweep ran only the failure case and read its output as a property of the page. THIS IS THE SECOND TIME TODAY THE SAME METHODOLOGICAL GAP FIRED. analytics was likewise recorded as 'silent under failure' when the injection pattern (`/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/`) never matched its `/functions/v1/` orchestrator path - and the page in fact says 'Analytics unavailable' with dashed heroes. A pass/fail over an untouched data path is the vacuous-injection shape the delayed-read probe already guards against by counting interceptions and refusing a verdict over zero; that guard belongs in the failure probe too, plus a healthy control on every page, which is now the standing method.

findings.title: FAILS: 8 call(s) failed and the page rendered EMPTINESS ("Nothing here") — a person cannot tell "there is nothing here" from "this did not load", and one of those is false. THE ORACLE IS A DIFFERENCE, NOT A STRING, inherited from the marketplace spec this extends: the page is read HEALTHY first, and
findings.detail: FAILS: 8 call(s) failed and the page rendered EMPTINESS ("Nothing here") — a person cannot tell "there is nothing here" from "this did not load", and one of those is false. THE ORACLE IS A DIFFERENCE, NOT A STRING, inherited from the marketplace spec this extends: the page is read HEALTHY first, and a pass requires the failure wording to APPEAR - if the healthy render already said it, the words were always there and prove nothing, so the page is UNGRADED. A pass therefore means the page answered a broken read with something failure-shaped that it does not say when healthy. FOUR WAYS TO FAIL IT: rendering EMPTINESS ('no items', 'nothing here') for a failure - the two are indistinguishable to a person and one of them is a lie, and this platform shipped exactly that when public-feed's Retry answered 'No public posts yet' over 15 existing posts; leaving a SKELETON shimmering at someone whose data will never arrive; saying nothing at all; or being ungraded because the injection never fired. The vocabulary is IMPORTED from session_signals.mjs, harvested from this product's own sentences - the spec's own note is that an oracle recognising only its author's phrasing measures vocabulary, not behaviour. ★ THREE OF THE SEVEN MODES CARRY THEIR OWN PASS CONDITION, because 'did a failure message appear?' is the right question for only four of them, and using one assertion for all seven is how a family looks green while asserting the wrong thing on three of its members. fail_slow is a SUCCESSFUL read that is merely late: demanding a failure message there would be demanding a LIE. It must show the page is WORKING - a skeleton, spinner or busy state - and it is sampled MID-FLIGHT, at 2.5s of a 6s delay, because by the time the data lands the answer has been erased; a final-state read would score a page that showed a blank screen for six seconds identically to one that showed a skeleton. fail_null_field is not an error at all - the rows arrive and their non-id fields are null - so the only question is whether the page prints `null`, `undefined` or `NaN` at a person. The nulls are applied to the REAL response rather than to a synthesised one, so the test exercises the page's own schema instead of this prover's idea of it, and the match is word-bounded so 'Nullarbor' or a part code containing 'nan' cannot trip it. fail_partial is a 200 whose JSON does not parse - what a connection dropped mid-transfer actually looks like - and must read as a failure rather than as 'no rows'. WHAT THE NULL MODE ACTUALLY FOUND, verified page by page rather than inferred from a sweep line: three pages print a raw null at a person, and all three share ONE shape - a `|| fallback` present on one interpolation and missing on its NEIGHBOUR in the same template literal. inventory:1542 `Available: ${item.qty_on_hand} ${item.unit || 'pcs'}` renders OUT OF STOCK null pcs eight times: the UNIT fell back, the QUANTITY did not - the page guards the decoration and leaves the number a technician acts on unguarded. alert-hub:611 `shift ${brief.shift_date} · model ${brief.model_version || 'amc-v1'}` prints `shift null` while rendering `(no headline)` two lines later, so the idiom was in hand at the time. skillmatrix:854 `Primary: ${_profile.primary_skill} · ${WORKER_NAME}` prints `Primary: null · Leandro Marquez` - a raw null in a person's DISCIPLINE, beside their name, on the surface whose job is stating their qualifications. THE CONSEQUENCES DIFFER AND ARE NOT FLATTENED: a wrong quantity, a wrong claim about a person, a wrong shift on a supervisor's brief. One habit, three one-token corrections - not a design decision. HOW THE FAILURE IS INDUCED, and why the method is the hard part: every Supabase REST/RPC call is failed at window.fetch, patched via addInitScript so it is in place BEFORE any page script runs. That timing is the whole trick. tests/failure-injection.spec.ts records that replacing window.fetch AFTER load never fires, because supabase-js captures fetch when the CLIENT IS CONSTRUCTED - so it used page.route instead; this project separately learned that page.route is bypassed by a warm SERVICE WORKER serving from cache. Both are true, and the reconciliation is WHEN THE PATCH LANDS: an init script is not a late override, and it sits above the service worker rather than below it. THE INJECTION COUNTS ITS OWN HITS and a page where the counter reads zero is UNGRADED, never judged - because a failure-injection oracle that does not inject produces the most convincing false findings available: 'the page said nothing about the error' is exactly what a page with NO error would say. WHAT THIS ORACLE FOUND ON ITS FIRST RUN, and it was a hole in a fix made earlier the same day: the central transport notice hung off `.then(res => ...)`, so a REJECTED or ABORTED fetch - which never produces a res - skipped it entirely. Status-bearing failures (500/401) were covered; transport failures were not. Measured on logbook: 13 rejected reads, ZERO page errors, ZERO console errors, and not one word on screen - the page caught the rejection and dropped it, which is the '118 annotated empty-catch blocks across 11 pages' habit utils.js already documents. FIXED at the transport in a `.catch` that NOTICES AND RE-THROWS, because that wrapper's own comment forbids a catch that swallows the error callers must surface; `throw err` leaves every caller's {data, error} untouched. Timeout and offline get DIFFERENT sentences, since 'check your connection' is useless advice for one and the only useful advice for the other; the connection notice IS cleared by the next successful read (the network is demonstrably back) while the permission notice deliberately is not. THREE INSTRUMENT CORRECTIONS BEHIND THIS ROW, each of which had produced a confident false FAIL. (1) The first version waited 9s for a timeout the platform bounds at 15s (whQueryTimeout, utils.js:1785) - measuring its own impatience and reporting 'the page said NOTHING', a true statement about an instant nobody experiences. (2) Widening the wait revealed that whQueryTimeout is adopted by only SIX surfaces (community, public-feed and the four marketplace pages), so on these 20 pages the only bound is the transport abort at WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS || 45000; rather than idle 45s per page the prover sets that documented knob to 4s, which utils.js:703 explicitly invites ('tune via window.WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS'). (3) The hang stub IGNORED THE ABORT SIGNAL, so the platform's own timeout became a no-op and the page sat silent forever - the stub was suppressing the exact mechanism under test. A fake fetch must emulate CANCELLATION, not just latency. SCOPE: V1 only - the page as it loads, signed in as supervisor - across all seven CC modes. The V2 view is a separate row and is NOT claimed here. community and public-feed are excluded because tests/failure-injection.spec.ts already walks them. NON-WRITING: only reads are failed; nothing is typed or submitted.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - fail_401: an expired session is not surfaced honestly on this page. THIS FAILS ON 17 OF 17 PAGES WALKED, and the fix is ADOPTION, not a new message
findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Injecting a 401 into this page's reads, the page does not tell the reader their session expired, does not name the session as the cause, and does not state the consequence for what they were doing. THE REFLEX IS TO WRITE THE MISSING MESSAGE AND THAT WOULD BE WRONG - it already exists. utils.js:1568 reads 'Your session expired, so nothing was saved. Sign in again and redo this step.' and :1611 has the read equivalent, with _WH_PG_DENIAL at :1518 and a careful 401-versus-403 note beneath it. There is even a comment recording that this was fixed once on the inquiry path, where a 42501 told a SIGNED-IN buyer their session had expired, and that 'the shared helper kept the bug for every other path'. Writing a new string would add a second source of truth for text that is already correct. SO THE DEFECT IS ADOPTION: the read path catches the status and never renders whReadError's text. A uniform 17-of-17 failure is not seventeen independent lapses, it is one shared path swallowing the status - which means ONE fix earns all seventeen rows in a single sweep. Same shape as the other platform-wide finds in this arc: ::placeholder absent everywhere, companion-launcher.js with no prefers-reduced-motion block at all. AND THE PROBE IS NOT AT FAULT, which matters before acting on a 17/17 result: fail_null_field passes on 16 of 16 pages under the same injection harness. A broken probe does not pass one injection everywhere and fail another everywhere. Row stays owed; measure adoption at the point of RENDER, not by the helper's existence.

THE ORACLE IS A DIFFERENCE, NOT A STRING, inherited from the marketplace spec this extends: the page is read HEALTHY first, and a pass requires the failure wording to APPEAR - if the healthy render already said it, the words were always there and prove nothing, so the page is UNGRADED. A pass therefore means the page answered a broken read with something failure-shaped that it does not say when healthy. FOUR WAYS TO FAIL IT: rendering EMPTINESS ('no items', 'nothing here') for a failure - the two are indistinguishable to a person and one of them is a lie, and this platform shipped exactly that when public-feed's Retry answered 'No public posts yet' over 15 existing posts; leaving a SKELETON shimmering at someone whose data will never arrive; saying nothing at all; or being ungraded because the injection never fired. The vocabulary is IMPORTED from session_signals.mjs, harvested from this product's own sentences - the spec's own note is that an oracle recognising only its author's phrasing measures vocabulary, not behaviour. ★ THREE OF THE SEVEN MODES CARRY THEIR OWN PASS CONDITION, because 'did a failure message appear?' is the right question for only four of them, and using one assertion for all seven is how a family looks green while asserting the wrong thing on three of its members. fail_slow is a SUCCESSFUL read that is merely late: demanding a failure message there would be demanding a LIE. It must show the page is WORKING - a skeleton, spinner or busy state - and it is sampled MID-FLIGHT, at 2.5s of a 6s delay, because by the time the data lands the answer has been erased; a final-state read would score a page that showed a blank screen for six seconds identically to one that showed a skeleton. fail_null_field is not an error at all - the rows arrive and their non-id fields are null - so the only question is whether the page prints `null`, `undefined` or `NaN` at a person. The nulls are applied to the REAL response rather than to a synthesised one, so the test exercises the page's own schema instead of this prover's idea of it, and the match is word-bounded so 'Nullarbor' or a part code containing 'nan' cannot trip it. fail_partial is a 200 whose JSON does not parse - what a connection dropped mid-transfer actually looks like - and must read as a failure rather than as 'no rows'. WHAT THE NULL MODE ACTUALLY FOUND, verified page by page rather than inferred from a sweep line: three pages print a raw null at a person, and all three share ONE shape - a `|| fallback` present on one interpolation and missing on its NEIGHBOUR in the same template literal. inventory:1542 `Available: ${item.qty_on_hand} ${item.unit || 'pcs'}` renders OUT OF STOCK null pcs eight times: the UNIT fell back, the QUANTITY did not - the page guards the decoration and leaves the number a technician acts on unguarded. alert-hub:611 `shift ${brief.shift_date} · model ${brief.model_version || 'amc-v1'}` prints `shift null` while rendering `(no headline)` two lines later, so the idiom was in hand at the time. skillmatrix:854 `Primary: ${_profile.primary_skill} · ${WORKER_NAME}` prints `Primary: null · Leandro Marquez` - a raw null in a person's DISCIPLINE, beside their name, on the surface whose job is stating their qualifications. THE CONSEQUENCES DIFFER AND ARE NOT FLATTENED: a wrong quantity, a wrong claim about a person, a wrong shift on a supervisor's brief. One habit, three one-token corrections - not a design decision. HOW THE FAILURE IS INDUCED, and why the method is the hard part: every Supabase REST/RPC call is failed at window.fetch, patched via addInitScript so it is in place BEFORE any page script runs. That timing is the whole trick. tests/failure-injection.spec.ts records that replacing window.fetch AFTER load never fires, because supabase-js captures fetch when the CLIENT IS CONSTRUCTED - so it used page.route instead; this project separately learned that page.route is bypassed by a warm SERVICE WORKER serving from cache. Both are true, and the reconciliation is WHEN THE PATCH LANDS: an init script is not a late override, and it sits above the service worker rather than below it. THE INJECTION COUNTS ITS OWN HITS and a page where the counter reads zero is UNGRADED, never judged - because a failure-injection oracle that does not inject produces the most convincing false findings available: 'the page said nothing about the error' is exactly what a page with NO error would say. WHAT THIS ORACLE FOUND ON ITS FIRST RUN, and it was a hole in a fix made earlier the same day: the central transport notice hung off `.then(res => ...)`, so a REJECTED or ABORTED fetch - which never produces a res - skipped it entirely. Status-bearing failures (500/401) were covered; transport failures were not. Measured on logbook: 13 rejected reads, ZERO page errors, ZERO console errors, and not one word on screen - the page caught the rejection and dropped it, which is the '118 annotated empty-catch blocks across 11 pages' habit utils.js already documents. FIXED at the transport in a `.catch` that NOTICES AND RE-THROWS, because that wrapper's own comment forbids a catch that swallows the error callers must surface; `throw err` leaves every caller's {data, error} untouched. Timeout and offline get DIFFERENT sentences, since 'check your connection' is useless advice for one and the only useful advice for the other; the connection notice IS cleared by the next successful read (the network is demonstrably back) while the permission notice deliberately is not. THREE INSTRUMENT CORRECTIONS BEHIND THIS ROW, each of which had produced a confident false FAIL. (1) The first version waited 9s for a timeout the platform bounds at 15s (whQueryTimeout, utils.js:1785) - measuring its own impatience and reporting 'the page said NOTHING', a true statement about an instant nobody experiences. (2) Widening the wait revealed that whQueryTimeout is adopted by only SIX surfaces (community, public-feed and the four marketplace pages), so on these 20 pages the only bound is the transport abort at WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS || 45000; rather than idle 45s per page the prover sets that documented knob to 4s, which utils.js:703 explicitly invites ('tune via window.WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS'). (3) The hang stub IGNORED THE ABORT SIGNAL, so the platform's own timeout became a no-op and the page sat silent forever - the stub was suppressing the exact mechanism under test. A fake fetch must emulate CANCELLATION, not just latency. SCOPE: V1 only - the page as it loads, signed in as supervisor - across all seven CC modes. The V2 view is a separate row and is NOT claimed here. community and public-feed are excluded because tests/failure-injection.spec.ts already walks them. NON-WRITING: only reads are failed; nothing is typed or submitted.

findings.title: OWED FOR A SCOPE REASON, and the scope reason is the whole point of this row.
findings.detail: OWED FOR A SCOPE REASON, and the scope reason is the whole point of this row. tools/prove_failure_injection.mjs was run against resume this session and graded 7 of 7 cells PASS - but its cells carry `page: resume` and NO view, so they measure the page's DEFAULT view. Those are V1's rows, and V1's seven are already green. Banking them onto V2 would be the one-measurement-swept-two-views error: the review sheet is a different surface with different failure paths, and a page-level reading says nothing about how a DIALOG behaves when its own calls fail. WHAT V1'S RUN ESTABLISHED, recorded here as context rather than as this row's evidence: 8 call(s) failed and the page said so: "OVINCE / REGION PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY ⚠️ Could not load your saved resu (healthy 1798 chars -> 1706 under injection, 8 intercepted call(s)). WHY THIS VIEW IS NOW REACHABLE AT ALL: tools/dialog_targets.mjs had resume:V2 marked notDrivable on the false ground that 'openReview() is module-scoped and not callable from the page' - it is exposed as window.WHResume.openReview, and correcting that entry unlocked the view for the ten provers that read the registry. The layout and a11y provers graded it immediately (and the layout run found three 24x24 checkboxes under the 44px floor, since fixed). The failure-injection prover is simply not view-scoped yet. WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS: a view-scoped mode for prove_failure_injection - open the target through the shared registry, THEN inject, and assert against the dialog's own subtree rather than the whole page. Without that scoping the two readings are indistinguishable, which is precisely how a page-level pass would come to stand in for a dialog nobody tested. Note also that a false-pass risk lives in the verdict string: it is a window of body text, so it can OPEN mid-label ('OVINCE / REGION PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY') while the real evidence sits later in the same window - I read that as a false pass at first, and checking showed the genuine message was there. Assert on the message, not on the window.

findings.title: RUN CORRECTLY AND STILL NOT BANKABLE - and the reason is an instrument limitation worth more than the seven verdicts it produced.
findings.detail: RUN CORRECTLY AND STILL NOT BANKABLE - and the reason is an instrument limitation worth more than the seven verdicts it produced. FIRST, A CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER NOTE ON THIS ROW: I recorded that prove_failure_injection needed a view-scoped mode added. It already HAS one - `--view V2`, with a v2Target() lookup off the shared registry and a scope that reads the DIALOG's subtree instead of document.body. I had simply run it without the flag and then written the missing feature into the row. Look for the existing move before specifying a new one. RUN SCOPED, THE VERDICTS WERE: 6 PASS and 1 FAIL (fail_slow: 'a 14s read showed NO busy indicator at 2.5s'). Neither half can be banked, because of what the numbers underneath them say. ★EVERY CELL REPORTS healthyChars = 204 AND badChars = 204. The view renders identical content whether the reads succeed or every one of them fails. That is not resilience - it is IMMUNITY, and it is an artifact of how the view is opened: the shared registry drives resume:V2 through window.WHResume.openReview(title, items, onConfirm) with FIXTURE items, so the sheet's content comes from the harness, not from the network. No injected failure can reach its data. SO THE SIX PASSES ARE VACUOUS in the strict sense this bank cares about: 'this view rendered no false empty state' is trivially true of a view that cannot be emptied by the injection, and the failure notice they credit is the PAGE's, which the V1 rows already cover. And THE ONE FAILURE IS EQUALLY SUSPECT: fail_slow reports no busy indicator at 2.5s, but nothing in the sheet is loading - it was fully painted by the fixture before injection began - so a spinner would have nothing to represent. Banking that red would file a defect the harness manufactured. THE GENERAL RULE, which applies to every openBy:'fn' target that carries a data payload: a failure-injection oracle cannot grade a view whose content the FIXTURE supplies. The injection and the view have to share a data path, or the reading says nothing in either direction. WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS: drive this view through its REAL pipeline - upload a file, let resume-extract answer, and inject on THAT call - so the checklist the sheet renders is the thing that fails. That path writes (resume_documents) and calls an AI edge function, which is precisely why the registry entry used to say the view was unreachable at all; the honest version is that it is reachable read-only for STRUCTURAL oracles (layout, a11y, escape - all graded green this session) and needs the real pipeline for DATA oracles like this family.

scenarios.oracle: a resume version is immutable once exported; editing creates a new version

evidence.asserts: Editing creates a NEW version and no path mutates an existing one. Two successive imports produced two distinct resume_versions rows (0 -> 2), each carrying its own doc snapshot and its own note, rather than one row being rewritten - so a version that has already been exported cannot change underneath the person who sent it. The immutability is structural rather than conventional: across the whole page there is NO update or upsert against resume_versions - only the insert in snapshotVersion and a prune that deletes the oldest beyond the most recent 10 - so there is no code path by which a stored snapshot's doc can be altered. snapshotVersion is called from 10 sites, ahead of the mutating actions, which is why an edit lands as a new row rather than in place. WORTH RECORDING: the prune means an exported version can eventually be DELETED once eleven newer snapshots exist. That is loss, not mutation - the oracle asks that a version not change, and it does not - but a person who exported version 1 and edited eleven times will no longer find it.
evidence.checked: Behaviourally, with the write counted in the database either side rather than inferred from the UI. Two runs were discarded rather than banked as failures: the first clicked a guessed confirm button that does not exist (the control is #review-confirm, 'Add selected'), and the second reached the real button but still wrote nothing - because snapshotVersion opens with 'if (!_resumeId || !_authUid) return' and the only resume_documents row belonged to a different worker, so the test identity had no resume to version. Seeding one made the test fire. Both the seeded document and every version row it produced were deleted, and both tables re-counted.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 6 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

evidence.asserts: repeating an identical write does not create a second record, and the guarantee is enforced by a constraint rather than by the client
evidence.checked: PROVEN BY REPEATING THE WRITE, inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member. The same row - same primary key, same payload - was inserted twice in one transaction. The second attempt was refused: 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint logbook_pkey'. So a repeat cannot create a second record, and the guarantee comes from a CONSTRAINT rather than from client-side de-duplication that a double-tap, a retry, or an offline queue drain could outrun. It renders 'Nothing here yet.' with no diagnosis, so there is nothing to retry and no reason given. SO THE ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant costs the whole page again on the connection that just failed. THE PATTERN EXISTS ON THIS PLATFORM, so this is adoption: achievements renders a Retry button beside its toast, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 post cards. Only 2 of 22 pages have one. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that RE-ISSUES the failed read - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY ANSWERING EVERY READ WITH A 500 AT window.fetch AND READING WHAT THE PAGE SAYS NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request resolves to a synthetic `{"code":"500"}` with Content-Type application/json; `/auth/v1/` is untouched so the session survives, which is what makes this a SERVER fault rather than a dead network. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. Every claim below quotes the page's own visible sentence, collected from leaf-ish elements under a composed-visibility test (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) so hidden template copy cannot be mistaken for something a reader sees. TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS SWEEP WERE THROWN AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE NUMBERS HERE ARE TRUSTED. The first used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered live data - a registered service worker sits between page and transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. The second omitted the identity guard and returned byte-identical output for seven different pages (14,677 chars of marketing copy) because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. This version guards INSIDE the evaluate: expected uid, `location.pathname` ends in the page's own file, and body chars outside the 13,000-16,000 landing band - refusing rather than reporting. findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

THE REVIEW SHEET ITSELF WRITES NOTHING. Its confirm handler captures the selected items and hands them to a caller-supplied onConfirm (the sheet is shared by the upload path and runAutofill), then closes - measured directly this session with window.WHResume.openReview and a spy callback: three presses produced exactly ONE invocation carrying the edited values, and no request left the page. What eventually stores the resume is saveCloud, and it already handles offline better than a refusal would: `if (!navigator.onLine) { toast('Offline: saved on this device, will sync later.'); await saveLocal(); return; }`. Nothing is lost and the person is told the truth. Notably this is the case that exposed a blind spot in the REGISTERED validator - its GUARD regex matched `navigator.onLine === false` but not the negation form `!navigator.onLine`, so this correct implementation was being reported as an unguarded write. Fixed this session; the selftest still passes all four cases. SO: green would credit a refusal that does not exist and must not; red would call the page's best behaviour a defect. WHAT THIS VIEW ACTUALLY OWES is the promise it makes twice in its own copy - that nothing enters the resume without confirmation - and that promise is already banked GREEN on this view's CO-ux-recovery rows (wrong_then_fix: unchecking dropped the confirm count 3->2 and the committed payload carried the EDITED text with the unchecked item excluded; did_it_land: the partial-extract case surfaces 'Read 2 of 3 sections - one page was busy'). findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

findings.title: the review sheet was never opened - this green rested on a builder-page reading, and reaching the view needs a real file upload through the extract path
findings.detail:
WHAT THE GREEN RESTED ON. Evidence identical to the V1 row's: a page-load reading of resume.html showing 5 reads in flight and 0 server-derived numeric writes. That is a measurement of the BUILDER, not of the review sheet, so the claim did not rest on what it names (R7). Twelve sibling V2 rows across the platform had the same fault and were repaired by measuring their views; this one could not be, and saying so is the honest outcome rather than leaving it green.

WHY THIS VIEW IS DIFFERENT FROM THE OTHER THIRTEEN. Every other V2 was reachable by a click, a tab, an anon context or an injected 500. '#review-sheet' (resume.html:256) is the extract-to-checklist confirm step, so reaching it requires a real document to travel the full path: browser-side parse (pdf.js / XLSX, resume.html:1109 and :1134) then the 'resume-extract' edge function, which resume.html:1140 reaches through a hand-rolled fetchWithTimeout rather than functions.invoke. No amount of arming the delay produces the view without a file going through that chain.

WHAT THE RE-WALK NEEDS, so the next session does not rediscover this. A fixture document (a small PDF or DOCX with one job entry) uploaded via the multi-file input at resume.html:218, with the delay armed BEFORE the extract call so the review sheet's own pending state is the one measured. The question to answer is whether the checklist asserts extracted content - a job title, a date, a skill - before the extract resolves, which on this page is the highest-stakes version of the oracle: the surface promises 'your files are read just to fill in your resume, then discarded', and a checklist row that appears before the read has landed is a claim about someone's employment history.

NOT A CEILING, A FIXTURE I DO NOT YET HAVE. The path is local and the upload is scriptable through browser_file_upload; what is missing is the fixture file, not access.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: a slow read is shown as slow - the page never answers with a server-derived value it does not have yet
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES: with 5 reads held in flight, **0 server-derived numbers were written**. This is a form surface with no numeric KPI tiles, so there is little to fabricate - stated so the pass is not read as stronger than it is. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any write to a data element stamped readsResolvedAtWrite === 0. Six pages on this platform do exactly that - asset-hub (`ah-*-hero`), report-sender (`rs-*-hero`), shift-brain (`sb-*-hero`), skillmatrix (`sm-*-hero`), achievements (`ac-*-hero`) and logbook - so the instrument is known to fire here when the fault is real. MEASURED BY DETECTING THE WRITE, WITH A POSITIVE CONTROL. Reads are wrapped in a 5s delay and counted on resolution; a MutationObserver records every mutation whose text is purely numeric, stamped with how many reads had resolved at that moment - so 'did the page write a number before it had the data?' is a measured fact. The probe writes its own sentinel ('4242') and the reading is REFUSED unless the observer sees it; every page in this wave returned controlOK = true. THE CONTROL EXISTS BECAUSE TWO EARLIER VERSIONS LIED IN THE FLATTERING DIRECTION - one tested only the added node's own text (missing numeric leaves inside an innerHTML render), the other never attached because `document.documentElement` was null at init-script time. Both reported 0 writes on pages that visibly populated. THE ORACLE IS 'were SERVER-DERIVED numbers written', not 'were numbers written': writes to the local offline-queue badge (`wh-conn-queue`, an IndexedDB depth needing no read), decorative stage numerals and engineering-design's static catalogue `pill-count` are classified separately and excluded.

evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: worker (own-documents boundary) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

evidence.asserts: no relation this page reads hides a refusal inside an empty successful response
evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 7 read relation(s), 2 were probed live at the gateway (resume_documents, resume_versions). None of them returns an identical status and body type to an anon caller and a member, so a refusal here is observably different from absence. THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.
